Advanced Machine Learning - Project Debrief
Visa Approval Facilitation

Problem Statement¶

Context:¶

Business communities in the United States are facing high demand for human resources, but one of the constant challenges is identifying and attracting the right talent, which is perhaps the most important element in remaining competitive. Companies in the United States look for hard-working, talented, and qualified individuals both locally as well as abroad.

The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) of the US permits foreign workers to come to the United States to work on either a temporary or permanent basis. The act also protects US workers against adverse impacts on their wages or working conditions by ensuring US employers' compliance with statutory requirements when they hire foreign workers to fill workforce shortages. The immigration programs are administered by the Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC).

OFLC processes job certification applications for employers seeking to bring foreign workers into the United States and grants certifications in those cases where employers can demonstrate that there are not sufficient US workers available to perform the work at wages that meet or exceed the wage paid for the occupation in the area of intended employment.

Objective:¶

In FY 2016, the OFLC processed 775,979 employer applications for 1,699,957 positions for temporary and permanent labor certifications. This was a nine percent increase in the overall number of processed applications from the previous year. The process of reviewing every case is becoming a tedious task as the number of applicants is increasing every year.

The increasing number of applicants every year calls for a Machine Learning based solution that can help in shortlisting the candidates having higher chances of VISA approval. OFLC has hired the firm EasyVisa for data-driven solutions. You as a data scientist at EasyVisa have to analyze the data provided and, with the help of a classification model:

  • Facilitate the process of visa approvals.
  • Recommend a suitable profile for the applicants for whom the visa should be certified or denied based on the drivers that significantly influence the case status.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of employee and the employer. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

  • case_id: ID of each visa application
  • continent: Information of continent the employee
  • education_of_employee: Information of education of the employee
  • has_job_experience: Does the employee has any job experience? Y= Yes; N = No
  • requires_job_training: Does the employee require any job training? Y = Yes; N = No
  • no_of_employees: Number of employees in the employer's company
  • yr_of_estab: Year in which the employer's company was established
  • region_of_employment: Information of foreign worker's intended region of employment in the US.
  • prevailing_wage: Average wage paid to similarly employed workers in a specific occupation in the area of intended employment. The purpose of the prevailing wage is to ensure that the foreign worker is not underpaid compared to other workers offering the same or similar service in the same area of employment.
  • unit_of_wage: Unit of prevailing wage. Values include Hourly, Weekly, Monthly, and Yearly.
  • full_time_position: Is the position of work full-time? Y = Full Time Position; N = Part Time Position
  • case_status: Flag indicating if the Visa was certified or denied

def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(15, 10), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (15,10))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a triangle will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram

# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 1, 5))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        palette="Paired",
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n].sort_values(),
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

### function to plot distributions wrt target


def distribution_plot_wrt_target(data, predictor, target):

    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))

    target_uniq = data[target].unique()

    axs[0, 0].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[0]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[0]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 0],
        color="teal",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[0, 1].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[1]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[1]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 1],
        color="orange",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[1, 0].set_title("Boxplot w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=target, y=predictor, ax=axs[1, 0], palette="gist_rainbow")

    axs[1, 1].set_title("Boxplot (without outliers) w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data,
        x=target,
        y=predictor,
        ax=axs[1, 1],
        showfliers=False,
        palette="gist_rainbow",
    )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(count + 5, 5))
    plt.legend(
        loc="lower left", frameon=False,
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.show()

Key Insights from Bivariate Analysis: 1. Visa Approval by Continent: • Applicants from Asia and North America have the highest number of approvals. • Africa and Oceania have the lowest approval rates. 2. Impact of Job Experience: • Candidates with job experience (Y) are significantly more likely to get their visa approved. • Those without experience (N) have a lower approval rate. 3. Prevailing Wage Across Regions: • Some regions (e.g., Northeast and West) have higher prevailing wages compared to others. • This could be a key factor influencing visa approvals. 4. Prevailing Wage and Visa Approval: • Candidates with higher wages seem to have a higher probability of visa approval. • However, some outliers indicate that high wages alone do not guarantee approval. 5. Unit of Wage and Visa Approval: • Yearly wages have the highest approval rate. • Hourly wages see a higher proportion of denials, possibly due to concerns about job stability.

Data Pre-processing¶

Outlier Check¶

  • Let's check for outliers in the data.
In [28]:
# outlier detection using boxplot
numeric_columns = data.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()


plt.figure(figsize=(15, 12))

for i, variable in enumerate(numeric_columns):
    plt.subplot(4, 4, i + 1)
    plt.boxplot(data[variable], whis=1.5)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.title(variable)

plt.show()

Interpretation of Outlier Detection Using Boxplots: 1. no_of_employees (Number of Employees) • Outliers detected: Many extreme values are present. • Some companies have an extremely high number of employees (e.g., over 600,000). • This might suggest the presence of large corporations, but could also be data entry errors. 2. yr_of_estab (Year of Establishment) • Outliers detected: Companies established before 1900 are considered extreme. • Most companies were established between 1950 and 2000, while a few were founded in the 1800s. • If very old companies are rare, they could be removed or transformed. 3. prevailing_wage (Salary) • Outliers detected: Some wages are exceptionally high (above 300,000). • Salaries vary significantly, likely due to differences in job types, industries, and locations. • Wage units (hourly, weekly, yearly) could also be affecting the distribution.

Next Steps & Actions: • For no_of_employees and prevailing_wage: • Consider capping extreme values (e.g., using the 99th percentile) or applying log transformation to handle skewness. • For yr_of_estab: • If older companies are legitimate, keep them. Otherwise, filter out unrealistic establishment years.

Data Preparation for modeling¶

  • We want to predict which visa will be certified.
  • Before we proceed to build a model, we'll have to encode categorical features.
  • We'll split the data into train and test to be able to evaluate the model that we build on the train data.

Model Building¶

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Provide some reasoning for choosing the metric here : ______

First, let's create functions to calculate different metrics and confusion matrix so that we don't have to use the same code repeatedly for each model.

  • The model_performance_classification_sklearn function will be used to check the model performance of models.
  • The confusion_matrix_sklearn function will be used to plot the confusion matrix.
In [31]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using sklearn


def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf
In [32]:
def confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors)
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

  1. Performance Ranking (Best to Worst) • GBM (Gradient Boosting Machine) – Best Performer • Shows the highest median score (~0.83). • The results are consistent (small variance), meaning the model is stable. • Adaboost and XGBoost – Strong Performers • XGBoost and Adaboost also show strong results (~0.82). • XGBoost is slightly more stable than Adaboost (narrower spread in the boxplot). • Random Forest – Good Performance • Performs well (~0.80) but slightly lower than GBM, Adaboost, and XGBoost. • It has a wider spread, meaning results vary across cross-validation runs. • Bagging – Moderate Performance • Has a lower median (~0.78), meaning it is less effective than boosting models. • Some variability in results across cross-validation. • Decision Tree (dtree) – Worst Performer • Lowest accuracy (~0.74). • Has a large spread, indicating inconsistent performance. • Suggests that a single tree model is too weak for this problem.

Insights & Recommendations 1. Best Models: GBM, Adaboost, and XGBoost • These models provide the best accuracy and stability. • Recommendation: Use GBM or XGBoost as the final model, and further optimize it with hyperparameter tuning. 2. Random Forest as a Backup Model • Random Forest is a good alternative, especially if computation time is a concern. • Can be fine-tuned with more trees to improve performance. 3. Avoid Using Decision Trees Individually • The Decision Tree (dtree) performs poorly due to high variance. • If used, it should be combined in an ensemble (Random Forest or GBM). 4. Fine-Tuning for Final Model • Apply Hyperparameter Tuning (GridSearchCV/RandomizedSearchCV) to GBM or XGBoost. • Test different learning rates, depth, and boosting parameters to further improve accuracy.

Insights from the Oversampling Data 1. Imbalanced Dataset Before Oversampling • Label ‘1’ (Certified cases): 11,913 (≈ 67%) • Label ‘0’ (Denied cases): 5,923 (≈ 33%) • Before applying oversampling, the dataset was imbalanced, meaning the model could be biased toward predicting “Certified” more often. 2. Balanced Dataset After Applying SMOTE • Label ‘1’ (Certified): 11,913 • Label ‘0’ (Denied): 11,913 • After Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE), the denied cases were increased to match the certified cases, ensuring a balanced dataset. 3. Impact of Oversampling on Model Performance • The training set size increased to 23,826 samples across 28 features. • A balanced dataset ensures that: • The model learns from both categories equally. • It reduces bias towards the majority class (“Certified”). • Better recall for the minority class (“Denied”), improving overall predictive power.

Performance Ranking (Best to Worst) • GBM (Gradient Boosting Machine) – Best Performer • Highest median performance (~0.825). • Small variance, meaning consistent performance across cross-validation runs. • XGBoost – Strong Performance • Performs almost as well as GBM (~0.82). • Slightly more variance than GBM, but still highly stable and accurate. • Random Forest – Good Alternative • Performs well (~0.80) but slightly lower than GBM and XGBoost. • Shows higher variance, meaning performance fluctuates across different folds. • Adaboost – Moderate Performance • Lower median (~0.795) compared to GBM and XGBoost. • Has a wider spread, indicating less stability. • Bagging – Below Average • Performance (~0.78) is lower than other ensemble models. • Not as strong as boosting-based models. • Decision Tree (DTree) – Worst Performer • Lowest performance (~0.73). • Highest variance, meaning it’s unstable. • Recommendation: Avoid using a single decision tree; instead, use an ensemble like Random Forest.

Recommendations: 1. Final Model Selection: • GBM or XGBoost should be used for final deployment. • Random Forest can be considered as a backup model. 2. Hyperparameter Tuning: • Fine-tune GBM and XGBoost for better performance. • Optimize parameters like learning rate, max depth, number of estimators, and regularization. 3. Monitor Precision vs Recall: • Since the dataset was oversampled, ensure that the model does not have too many false positives. • Use F1-score and AUC-ROC to balance precision and recall.

###Analysis of Training Performance

1. XGBoost Excels in Training Metrics • XGBoost exhibits the highest Accuracy (0.8536), Recall (0.9046), Precision (0.8209), and F1 (0.8607). • This suggests that, on the training set, XGBoost is capturing patterns more effectively than the other models. 2. Gradient Boosting: Strong Contender • Gradient Boosting also performs well with an Accuracy of 0.8326 and an F1 of 0.8404. • It trails XGBoost but still demonstrates a robust balance of Precision and Recall. 3. AdaBoost: Moderate Performance • While its Recall (0.8561) is competitive, Accuracy (0.7968) and F1 (0.8082) are somewhat lower than GBM and XGBoost. • It can still be a viable option, especially if computational simplicity is a factor. 4. Random Forest with Undersampling: Lowest Scores • Shows the lowest Accuracy (0.7336) and F1 (0.7411). • Undersampling likely removed too many samples, causing the model to underfit.

Gradient Boosting tuned with oversampled data XGBoost tuned with oversampled data AdaBoost tuned with oversampled data Random forest tuned with undersampled data
Accuracy 0.735136 0.730484 0.729757 0.712604
Recall 0.850892 0.853940 0.852416 0.734436
Precision 0.774673 0.768312 0.768295 0.816751
F1 0.810996 0.808866 0.808173 0.773410

Overall Comparison: • Gradient Boosting (GBM) tuned with oversampled data: • Accuracy: 0.735 • Recall: 0.851 • Precision: 0.775 • F1 Score: 0.811 (Highest) • XGBoost tuned with oversampled data: • Accuracy: 0.730 • Recall: 0.854 (Slightly higher) • Precision: 0.768 • F1 Score: 0.809 • AdaBoost tuned with oversampled data: • Accuracy: 0.730 • Recall: 0.852 • Precision: 0.768 • F1 Score: 0.808 • Random Forest tuned with undersampled data: • Accuracy: 0.713 (Lowest) • Recall: 0.734 (Much lower) • Precision: 0.817 (Highest) • F1 Score: 0.773

Key Observations: • Boosting Models with Oversampling: • GBM, XGBoost, and AdaBoost all exhibit strong performance metrics with high recall and F1 scores. • Although XGBoost and AdaBoost achieve a marginally higher recall, GBM provides the best overall balance with the highest F1 score, which indicates a good trade-off between precision and recall. • Random Forest with Undersampling: • This model shows the highest precision, meaning when it predicts a positive (Certified), it is more likely correct. • However, its recall is significantly lower, leading to a poorer F1 score. This suggests that undersampling might have removed too much information, adversely affecting the model’s ability to identify positives.

Recommendations:¶

  1.	Adopt Boosting with Oversampling:
      •	Gradient Boosting (GBM) tuned with oversampled data is recommended due to its superior F1 score (0.811), indicating it best balances recall and precision.
      •	Oversampling appears to be more effective than undersampling in this context, as it helps preserve valuable information from the minority class while enhancing overall model performance.
  2.	Further Fine-Tuning:
      •	Although the differences among GBM, XGBoost, and AdaBoost are small, consider further fine-tuning the hyperparameters around the best performing GBM settings to potentially improve the metrics even further.
  3.	Evaluate Business Requirements:
      •	If your primary concern is to minimize false negatives (i.e., not missing out on true certified cases), then a model with high recall (like XGBoost or AdaBoost) could be considered.
      •	However, if a balance between precision and recall is critical, the current GBM model offers the best overall performance.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

Power Ahead

Analysis of Feature Importances¶

1.	Education is a Major Driver:
    •	education_of_employee_High School ranks as the most important feature, indicating that applicants with only a high school diploma exhibit significantly different approval probabilities compared to higher education levels.
    •	Other education-related features (Bachelor’s, Master’s, Doctorate) also appear prominently, suggesting that educational attainment heavily influences the visa decision.
2.	Job Experience Matters:
    •	Both has_job_experience_Y (and presumably its counterpart has_job_experience_N) appear near the top.
    •	This implies that work experience is a key factor—candidates with relevant experience may have higher chances of approval.
3.	Wage Type Over Wage Amount:
    •	unit_of_wage_Hour is notably important, whereas prevailing_wage itself appears lower on the list.
    •	This suggests the type of wage (hourly, weekly, monthly, yearly) may have a stronger predictive influence than the actual wage amount. Possibly, certain wage types correlate with job roles that have higher or lower approval rates.
4.	Geographical Factors:
    •	continent_Europe, region_of_employment_South, and region_of_employment_West are moderately important.
    •	This reflects regional and continental differences in visa approvals—some areas or origins may be more favorable than others.
5.	Less Impactful Features:
    •	yr_of_estab, no_of_employees, unit_of_wage_Month, and some specific continents (e.g., continent_Africa, continent_Oceania) are near the bottom, indicating minimal effect on the model’s decisions.

Recommendations¶

1.	Focus on Education & Experience:
    •	If applicants have limited formal education or no job experience, highlighting additional certifications or specialized skills might improve approval rates.
    •	Employers might consider supporting educational or training programs to enhance applicants’ profiles.
2.	Wage Structure Review:
    •	The strong impact of unit_of_wage_Hour suggests hourly wage positions may correlate differently with approvals than salaried (yearly) roles.
    •	Employers could explore aligning wage structures with positions that historically have higher approval rates.
3.	Leverage Regional Insights:
	•	Since region_of_employment and continent are moderately important, applicants or employers could consider how certain locations might affect visa chances.
    •	Policy variations or demand in specific regions could be influencing these outcomes.
